bridges.description: Show that historical Bibles sometimes attribute non-original wording to Jesus.
Show that a recoverable ancestor need not reproduce the autograph.
Show that some viable variants materially affect interpretation.
Explain why uncertainty challenged Ehrman’s former inspiration view.
Show that variants are not misquotations because wording and message remain recoverable.
Show that distributed transmission preserves readings without central control.
Distinguish raw totals from meaningful viable variants and message continuity.
Show that perfect copies or unanimous certainty are not required.

sections.title: Copying history and variant scale
sections.rationale: Frames the historical copying problem and the limited meaning of the raw variant total.

sections.title: Additions, sayings, and message continuity
sections.rationale: Covers major added passages, disputed sayings, and whether local variants remove the broader message.

sections.title: Preservation, tenacity, and genealogy
sections.rationale: Tests distributed transmission, persistence of readings, early witness support, P75, and a possible pre-branch bottleneck.

sections.title: Mark and Hebrews variant tests
sections.rationale: Keeps the reciprocal internal, external, local-meaning, and whole-book arguments for the two central examples together.

sections.title: Comparison denominators and historical certainty
sections.rationale: Separates printed editions from manuscripts and compares semantic and historical standards.

sections.title: Inspiration, preservation, and the motion
sections.rationale: Distinguishes the personal inspiration argument, apostolic practice, and each closing answer to the motion.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Successive hand copies inherited and added mistakes while originals disappeared.
moves.warrant: Ehrman joins inherited errors, new errors, and loss of correcting exemplars.
moves.inference: Survivors cannot simply be assumed to preserve every original word.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 144–209 begin when Ehrman states that the first copy made mistakes and end after he completes the sequence of inherited errors, attempted corrections, and loss of the original and early copies.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 144–283 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The copying mechanism matters because inherited errors plus lost exemplars explain why a large surviving tradition can still depart from the originals.

burdenContact.rationale: The pro recovery route depends on whether the copying process could sever surviving wording from the lost originals; this move supplies that mechanism.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The woman-taken-in-adultery story was inserted by scribes rather than originally written in John.
moves.warrant: Ehrman says the passage is absent from the oldest authorities despite its popularity.
moves.inference: A famous Jesus story can appear in Bibles without being original New Testament text.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 591–651 begin with Ehrman’s insertion claim and end after his manuscript-based conclusion; the intervening narrative is needed to identify the exact story whose textual status he disputes.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 591–651 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The adultery story is a concrete, familiar passage that entered later copies, showing that a beloved unit can be absent from the earliest recoverable text.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro misquotation status by identifying a whole passage printed as scripture although it was not in the earliest recoverable Gospel text.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The final twelve verses of Mark were added after the Gospel originally ended at 16:8.
moves.warrant: Ehrman contrasts the abrupt ending with the later resurrection appearances and signs absent from the oldest witnesses.
moves.inference: A substantial block about Jesus can be transmitted as Scripture although it was not original to Mark.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 652–715 contain the original-ending claim, the content supplied by the added ending, and the conclusion about the oldest witnesses; all three identify the load-bearing example.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 652–715 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Mark’s longer ending supplies resurrection appearances and signs, so its later addition bears directly on whether every printed Gospel passage preserves Mark’s wording.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro misquotation status because the familiar ending attributes material to Mark that the earliest evidence does not.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The prayer from the cross and the end-times saying contain disputed words attributed directly to Jesus.
moves.warrant: Ehrman notes omissions in early manuscripts for Luke 23:34 and Matthew 24.
moves.inference: At some sayings, which words Jesus is represented as speaking depends on the manuscript.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 717–765 contain two short saying examples and Ehrman’s concluding uncertainty claim; the pair supports the motion without repeating the longer added-passage cases.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 717–765 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The disputed sayings turn the textual question into a historical one: some words printed as Jesus’ speech may not have been written by the evangelists.

burdenContact.rationale: This reaches the motion’s attribution bridge by arguing that later textual additions can be presented as words of Jesus.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: More manuscripts produce more variants while providing more reconstructive evidence.
moves.warrant: White links abundance to both the count and confidence from early varied witnesses.
moves.inference: The headline total is misleading without historical context.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 868–926 begin with White’s summary of the raw-variant argument and end after his completed inference that manuscript abundance can increase both variants and reconstructive evidence; later taxonomy is separately inventoried.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 868–940 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: White’s count comparison is needed to test whether the headline number of variants is meaningful without relating it to the size and repetition of the manuscript tradition.

burdenContact.rationale: This bears on the con significance route because a raw variant total is probative only after accounting for the unusually large corpus being compared.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Only a limited subset of variants is both meaningful and viable, and many differences have ordinary scribal explanations.
moves.warrant: White distinguishes non-meaningful, nonviable, accidental, harmonized, and purposeful changes before estimating the relevant subset.
moves.inference: The existence of variants does not make every variant a plausible alternative affecting interpretation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 955–1027 supply White’s complete classification and the estimate that depends on it; stopping earlier would omit viability, while starting later would conceal the denominator.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 955–1027 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The category distinction identifies the disputed remainder after spelling, nonsense readings, and readings confined to a single witness are removed.

burdenContact.rationale: This narrows the con significance burden to variants that are both possible and consequential rather than treating every copied difference alike.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: The earliest witnesses display multiple intersecting transmission lines rather than one centrally edited chain.
moves.warrant: White says varied lines and the absence of a controlling editor make coordinated wholesale alteration less plausible.
moves.inference: Distributed transmission supplies independent comparative evidence for reconstruction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1029–1055 contain White’s early-witness count claim, the multiple-line inference, and the no-central-control consequence, ending before the distinct P75 illustration.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1029–1055 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: Independent early transmission lines without a central editor are White’s reason that agreement among geographically separated witnesses can preserve an ancient reading.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery by offering independent transmission lines as evidence that no central authority could uniformly rewrite the text.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Representative printed Byzantine and critical texts agree on more than 95 percent of words.
moves.warrant: White distinguishes printed texts from manuscripts and reports under 6,600 differences.
moves.inference: Representative textual forms retain substantial continuity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1091–1155 contain the printed-edition limitation, samples, difference figure, and inference; removing one would blur the denominator.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1091–1155 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: The comparison between representative Byzantine and critical New Testament editions measures how much wording differs between two prominent reconstructed textual forms.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports the con continuity route by using two representative New Testament printed editions to quantify how much of their wording agrees.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Once a reading enters the manuscript tradition it tends to persist, including errors and nonsense readings.
moves.warrant: White uses textual tenacity and the extra-puzzle-pieces analogy to argue that original readings remain among surviving alternatives.
moves.inference: Reconstruction usually selects among extant readings rather than inventing a missing option.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1156–1204 state the persistence premise, draw the inference to surviving originals, give the puzzle analogy, and distinguish that claim from an absolute-certainty standard.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1156–1204 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Tenacity is a separate preservation premise: once readings enter the manuscript stream, they tend to persist, leaving later critics evidence to compare rather than erasing alternatives.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery because persistent readings remain available for comparison even after competitors arise.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Whether Mark says Jesus became angry or felt compassion creates a real local interpretive difference.
moves.warrant: Ehrman contrasts the two emotions while placing the example among a limited set of consequential variants.
moves.inference: The reading affects how Mark portrays Jesus at that episode.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1711–1718 state the complete anger-versus-love contrast and Ehrman’s conclusion that the difference is substantive; later exchanges supply, rather than replace, its evidential defense.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1711–1718 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The anger/compassion variant changes Jesus’ portrayed emotion and therefore supplies a focused test of whether a single-word variant can matter to interpretation.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro significance with a variant that changes the described mental state of Jesus.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Ehrman’s former inspiration view became difficult because some original wording was uncertain.
moves.warrant: He says a God ensuring authors’ words could ensure preservation, while calling this personal rather than the main point.
moves.inference: For his former theology, uncertainty counted against verbal inspiration.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1841–1892 preserve both the preservation argument and Ehrman’s explicit limitation that it is personal motivation rather than the central textual burden.
moves.attributionRationale: Events 1841–1891 are Ehrman’s closing portion of the rebuttal; event 1892 supplies his final word “yes” before White begins, and only Ehrman’s words are credited.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Ehrman’s former inerrancy doctrine explains the actual standard he says the evidence defeated: divine inspiration without exact preservation no longer secured the words.

burdenContact.rationale: This supplies the pro standard bridge: exact wording mattered because Ehrman’s inspiration doctrine treated the original words as divinely given.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: White’s claimed number of manuscripts within a century is not established by the examples and dating offered in cross-examination.
moves.warrant: Ehrman asks for the twelve witnesses; White cites Wallace, Comfort, Skeat, P52 and P32 but does not supply the complete list, and the dating remains contested.
moves.inference: The asserted early-witness quantity cannot carry more weight than its stated support in this debate.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2281–2373 retain the exact numerical question, White’s cited basis and examples, Ehrman’s dating challenge, and the immediate correction from 200 to 120; shortening it would remove a necessary qualification.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage alternates speakers. Ehrman owns the requests for the twelve manuscripts, the dating objections, and the correction challenge; White’s citations and numerical correction are retained only as the answers being tested.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: The scarcity of very early witnesses directly tests whether later numerical abundance can establish what the first copies said.

burdenContact.rationale: This challenges con recovery at its weakest chronological point: the relative lack of witnesses close to the originals.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman challenges White’s appeal to numerous early, varied witnesses by disputing how many cited manuscripts actually fall within the first century after composition and what the uncertain dates establish.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: A word-agreement figure for representative printed editions is different from agreement among individual manuscripts at variant units.
moves.warrant: The cross-examination distinguishes printed reconstructed texts, individual manuscript collations, total words, and percentages used to group manuscripts.
moves.inference: The 95 percent figure cannot be transferred unchanged to a different evidence type or denominator.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2375–2478 are needed because the parties repeatedly clarify what is being compared; the complete exchange preserves White’s printed-text limitation and Ehrman’s distinct manuscript question.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage alternates speakers. Ehrman owns the manuscript-versus-printed-text and variant-unit-versus-all-word questions; White’s repeated printed-text clarification is context and receives no pro credit.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Separating printed editions, manuscript witnesses, and total copied words prevents a favorable percentage from changing denominators midargument.

burdenContact.rationale: This challenges con significance by showing that percentages based on printed editions or total words do not directly measure uncertainty among actual manuscripts.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman accepts that representative printed editions can show high word agreement but argues that this does not measure agreement among individual manuscripts at the places where they vary.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Close agreement between P75 and Vaticanus shows one stable related stream but does not represent every early witness or establish copying in the first century.
moves.warrant: Ehrman contrasts other manuscripts from P75’s period and asks what fourth-century copying tells us about the year 70.
moves.inference: The pair cannot by itself close the gap before surviving witnesses.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2604–2623 contain Ehrman’s concession that the pair shows a consistent Proto-Alexandrian stream and his precise question about extrapolating that result back to the earliest period.
moves.attributionRationale: Ehrman owns the concession about a stable related stream and the question what later copying proves about year 70; White’s answer begins after this selected span.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: One unusually close papyrus–codex pairing cannot by itself establish that the missing early tradition as a whole was equally stable.

burdenContact.rationale: This challenges con recovery by denying that P75 can stand in for the largely missing early manuscript population.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: P75 and Vaticanus illustrate related yet non-parent-child witnesses within a wider pattern of multiple lines.
moves.warrant: White explains that the pair is unusually close but not a direct copy relationship, and treats that pattern across witnesses as placing a burden on primitive-corruption claims.
moves.inference: Independent descent within a related stream contributes evidence even though it does not itself prove direct access to the autograph.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2624–2658 are White’s answer to the year-70 question through his clarification that ‘line’ meant no direct parent-child copying; the span preserves his actual limited inference.
moves.attributionRationale: White owns the answer about unusual closeness, non-parent-child descent, and multiple lines. Ehrman’s brief interruptions clarify the meaning of ‘line’ but are not credited to White.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: White uses P75’s agreement with Vaticanus across time, together with other transmission lines, as affirmative evidence against unrestricted early change.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery by treating P75–Vaticanus agreement as one dated example within several independently attested textual lines.

responseComponents.description: White answers the representativeness objection by treating P75 and Vaticanus as related but non-parent-child evidence within a larger set of transmission lines, rather than claiming that P75 alone represents every early witness.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The possibility that an extant reading is original does not establish that the original always survives among the alternatives.
moves.warrant: Ehrman distinguishes possibility from probability and offers 1 Peter 3:19 as a plausible conjectural-emendation case rather than a demonstrated lost original.
moves.inference: Tenacity needs an evidential argument beyond the logical possibility of an extant original reading.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2805–2866 include White’s exact tenacity challenge, Ehrman’s possibility/probability distinction, and the qualified conjectural example needed to avoid overstating it.
moves.attributionRationale: White asks whether any extant options exclude the original; Ehrman owns the possibility/probability distinction and conjectural-emendation example. Only Ehrman’s answer is scored.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The exchange exposes the limit of tenacity: persistence helps only if an original reading survives somewhere, while conjectural emendation addresses cases where it may not.

burdenContact.rationale: This tests the con tenacity bridge against the possibility that no surviving witness retains the original reading.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman distinguishes the possibility that an original reading persists from proof that it does, pointing to conjectural emendation as evidence that critics sometimes consider all surviving readings secondary.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Overall word agreement cannot measure semantic importance because one negation can reverse meaning.
moves.warrant: One word in a hundred-word statement may determine the whole sentence.
moves.inference: High aggregate agreement does not settle particular disputes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2867–2887 are the complete compact answer: refusal of a raw percentage is immediately supported by the single-negation semantic example.
moves.attributionRationale: The span is a mixed cross-examination exchange. The scored voice is Bart Ehrman: the claim and warrant describe only Bart Ehrman’s questions or answers, while the opponent’s words supply the immediate context and are excluded from credit and quotation.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Ehrman’s examples show that the remaining uncertainty can alter meaning even if most variants are trivial.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro significance because the disputed remainder can affect translation and interpretation rather than only spelling.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman argues that a high overall percentage of identical words does not settle significance because a single changed word, such as a negation, can reverse a sentence’s meaning.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Hebrews 2:9 either explicitly says Jesus died apart from God or explicitly presents his death as an act of divine grace.
moves.warrant: Ehrman argues that neither explicit formulation appears elsewhere in Hebrews in the same way.
moves.inference: The variant changes a distinctive teaching at that verse even if related themes occur elsewhere.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2888–2903 are Ehrman’s complete answer identifying the two readings, their distinct theological senses, and the claimed absence of the grace formulation elsewhere in Hebrews.
moves.attributionRationale: White asks for an example before this span; events 2888–2903 are Ehrman’s answer describing the two Hebrews readings and their explicit theological difference.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Hebrews 2:9 provides a direct lexical contrast—Jesus dies by divine grace or apart from God—so the variant cannot be dismissed as mere spelling.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro significance through two competing readings with expressly different claims about God’s relation to Jesus’ death.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: A reading consistent with Hebrews cannot straightforwardly be said to change the entire message of Hebrews.
moves.warrant: White presses Ehrman’s own earlier claim that ‘apart from God’ fits Hebrews and distinguishes local explicit wording from whole-book theology.
moves.inference: The example may alter one explicit statement without transforming the book’s overall message.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2904–2934 contain White’s consistency question and the ensuing clarification of local explicit teaching versus the book’s wider atonement theme, including the limited witness qualification.
moves.attributionRationale: White owns the consistency and whole-book questions. Ehrman’s intervening clarifications are retained to identify what White is testing but are not presented as White’s claims.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: White argues that the Hebrews variant must be weighed against the theology of the whole book, even though the two local readings make different explicit statements.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con significance by asking whether a changed explicit verse changes Hebrews’ overall teaching when the contested idea is otherwise consistent with the book.

responseComponents.description: White does not deny the local wording difference; he argues that its force must be assessed against Hebrews’ teaching as a whole.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Applying Ehrman’s uncertainty language consistently to worse-attested classical works would make ordinary historical quotation appear equally doubtful.
moves.warrant: White asks how the much longer gaps for Suetonius and others should be described and whether a parallel ‘misquoting’ critique follows.
moves.inference: The textual standard should not be applied more skeptically to the New Testament than to other ancient sources.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2941–2954 contain White’s complete comparative challenge, Ehrman’s concession that the classical gap is even larger, and White’s question about applying the same title and standard.
moves.attributionRationale: White owns the question applying Ehrman’s standard to classical gaps; Ehrman’s ‘ginormous’ answer is context confirming the premise, not part of White’s credited warrant.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The comparison asks whether the same amount of uncertainty would make nonbiblical ancient literature unusable, a direct test of the skeptical consequence being urged.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con proportionality by asking whether Ehrman’s standard would also discredit historically usable classical texts.

responseComponents.description: White tests the consequence of Ehrman’s admitted uncertainty about exact original wording by asking whether the same standard would make ordinary quotation of more sparsely attested classical works untenable.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The same uncertainty about exact original wording applies to classical literature without preventing responsible use of surviving witnesses.
moves.warrant: Ehrman says specialists openly discuss uncertain readings and that quotations refer to the manuscript tradition rather than an extant autograph.
moves.inference: Uncertainty at some words does not entail total skepticism about ancient history.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2955–3005 are Ehrman’s sustained answer: scholars study textual uncertainty, still quote surviving traditions, and reject claims of absolute recovery rather than all historical knowledge.
moves.attributionRationale: Ehrman owns the answer that classical specialists acknowledge uncertainty while still using manuscript traditions; White’s questions are context only.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Ehrman’s answer fixes the scope of his conclusion: ancient texts remain historically usable while particular words and passages remain uncertain.

burdenContact.rationale: This preserves pro significance while rejecting total skepticism: usability does not remove uncertainty about specific words.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman answers that classical texts remain historically usable while scholars still acknowledge uncertainty about their exact original wording.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Continued scholarly quotation of classical authors shows that a sufficiently clear text can be used despite acknowledged uncertainty.
moves.warrant: White presses whether Ehrman still cites Suetonius and treats the surviving form as usable evidence.
moves.inference: Historical use therefore does not require perfect recovery of every original word.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2973–2980 contain White’s question whether acknowledged uncertainty nevertheless leaves sufficiently clear knowledge to quote Suetonius and Ehrman’s immediate qualified answer. This interleaved question occurs within the longer classical-uncertainty exchange; the opening carryover word “said” and Ehrman’s answer are context, not White’s authored claim.
moves.attributionRationale: White owns the question from “so when” in event 2973 through “quote suetonius don’t you” in event 2977. Ehrman’s “yes of course” and explanation through event 2980 are a response used as context; no words from that answer are attributed to White.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: White turns Ehrman’s concession into a narrower conclusion that textual uncertainty does not entail wholesale textual unreliability.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con proportionality by using the conceded historical usability of ancient texts to limit the force of textual uncertainty.

responseComponents.description: White uses Ehrman’s concession about responsible classical quotation to argue that acknowledged textual uncertainty does not make a surviving text unusable.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: The anger reading rests on an unusually free witness and may have arisen by harmonizing nearby strong language.
moves.warrant: White invokes Bezae’s isolated character and proposes that a scribe imported anger from the surrounding context.
moves.inference: External support and a plausible source of alteration weigh against Ehrman’s preferred reading.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 3041–3087 contain White’s complete external-evidence question and his contextual harmonization proposal, ending when Ehrman begins his substantive internal-evidence answer.
moves.attributionRationale: White owns the external-evidence and harmonization challenge. Ehrman’s acknowledgments about Bezae are included only where they answer White’s questions and are not counted as White’s evidence.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: White offers a rival origin for the anger reading: a scribe may have imported nearby strong language into an unusually free witness, rather than compassion arising by softening anger.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery by combining the anger reading’s thin external support with White’s proposal that nearby strong language prompted its addition.

responseComponents.description: White accepts that anger and compassion differ locally but challenges anger’s originality through its limited external support and a proposed nearby source for scribal addition.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Internal evidence favors the harder anger reading even though the result adds nuance rather than changing the entire Gospel.
moves.warrant: Ehrman says his case does not rest on Bezae generally, argues compassion is an understandable scribal softening, and limits the effect to a fuller picture of Markan anger.
moves.inference: The variant is locally meaningful without proving wholesale message change.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 3088–3133 preserve Ehrman’s internal-evidence answer, proposed direction of change, and explicit ‘different nuance’ limitation; all are required for a fair reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Ehrman owns the internal-evidence defense, proposed direction of scribal change, and nuance limitation. White’s prompt at the boundary supplies context only.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Ehrman answers with Mark’s own pattern of Jesus becoming angry and limits the claim to the reading best explaining the alternatives, rather than certainty.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro method by using Markan usage to explain why compassion could have replaced anger while openly limiting the certainty claimed.

responseComponents.description: Ehrman answers White’s external and harmonization case with Mark’s recurring portrayal of Jesus’ anger, while limiting his conclusion to a nuanced local characterization.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Multiple later branches can descend from an already altered common copy.
